lead.kicker: Ajay Shah and Amit Varma on three audacious firms
lead.head: Giant leaps for firmkind

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 22

body: Ajay Shah once claimed ex­per­tise in six­teen things, and Amit Varma, re­port­ing that “hash­tags have been formed”, de­manded at least one more. Shah’s an­swer was firms[[x1]]. {022-J01}

Firms nor­mally grow by economies of scale, doing more of what they know, or by economies of scope, mov­ing into ad­ja­cen­cies. Three firms, Shah said, did not fit any stan­dard con­cep­tion of how firms grow.

Sun Microsystems, Google and Amazon did nei­ther. “It was not economies of scale, it was not re­ally economies of scope, and it was jump­ing to some­thing way more com­pli­cated,” Shah said. {022-C01}
## Three jumps

In the late 1980s, Sun as­sem­bled work­sta­tions from Motorola CPUs and off-the-shelf parts. When Motorola hit a wall, Sun began de­sign­ing its own CPUs, and in­vented a new ar­chi­tec­ture, SPARC. {022-S01}

Google started as a search en­gine and came to see it­self as an in­fra­struc­ture com­pany. Then it took on Android, which Andy Rubin brought to it. An op­er­at­ing sys­tem, Shah said, is the most com­plex piece of soft­ware. {022-S02}

Amazon, by his ac­count doing “the dullest thing in the world” as an on­line book­shop, began rent­ing out the com­put­ers it had bought for the Christmas rush, and ef­fec­tively in­vented cloud com­put­ing. {022-S03}
So a com­puter maker, a search com­pany and a book­shop each jumped, in Shah’s words, into “the world’s most com­plex thing”.
## The nerve to jump

What made the leaps pos­si­ble? Shah listed in­ter­nal cash flows and the love of fi­nan­cial mar­kets, in­sid­ers ask­ing hard ques­tions about threats, and lead­ers with deep en­gi­neer­ing cred­i­bil­ity.

At Sun, he said, Bill Joy and Andreas Bechtolsheim were so re­spected that es­sen­tially any­body in the world would have joined them. Google, in his telling, in­her­ited a Unix cul­ture that ran from Sun through Netscape.

“Execution is com­modi­tized,” Shah said. Mainstream Indian firm cul­ture, he ar­gued, ob­sesses over it and over obe­di­ent peo­ple, and is weak in strate­gic think­ing: part of what makes India a poor coun­try.
He also checked him­self for sur­vivor­ship bias, ask­ing whether many firms had leapt and a few landed by dumb luck. Having watched these three for years, he still thinks they were spe­cial.
## Leaps of imag­i­na­tion

Varma ob­jected to “just a book­shop”. Imagining a book­shop on the in­ter­net, he said, was it­self a spec­tac­u­lar leap. For him, such leaps owe more to cre­ative sto­ry­telling than to lin­ear busi­ness logic.
A good busi­ness leader can be made with an MBA, ex­e­cu­tion and in­cen­tives, he said. A great one needs to be an artist, able to tell a new story about what the firm re­ally is.

His ex­am­ples in­cluded the val­u­a­tion ex­pert Aswath Damodaran, who changed his mind about Uber after Bill Gurley told him he had the wrong story, and Netflix, which moved to stream­ing at the peak of its DVD busi­ness.

The rec­om­men­da­tions turned to the craft be­hind such leaps. Shah chose Tracy Kidder’s *The Soul of a New Machine*, his first glimpse, when young, of en­gi­neer­ing done with all your heart and soul.

Varma read from Rick Rubin’s *The Creative Act*: turn­ing an idea into re­al­ity can make it seem smaller. Shah said he sees the op­po­site, with work be­com­ing more beau­ti­ful at every pass. “So I al­ways love my ba­bies much bet­ter at the end than at the be­gin­ning,” he said.
“Because young ba­bies are a pain,” Varma replied.

second.label: The Uber valuation
second.head: Wrong story, wrong price
second.deck: Amit Varma on how Aswath Damodaran changed his mind about Uber, publicly

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the Uber valuation

body: Around 2014, the val­u­a­tion ex­pert Aswath Damodaran wrote a scep­ti­cal post on Uber. His story, Amit Varma said, was that Uber was in the taxi and car-service busi­ness, a mar­ket of $100 bil­lion, of which it would get at most 10 per cent. {#tam}
Bill Gurley, a leg­endary in­vestor and an early backer of Uber, replied that Damodaran had the wrong story. Uber was out to re­place car own­er­ship, a far big­ger mar­ket. {022-R05}

Damodaran agreed in pub­lic that Gurley was right, which Varma held up as a model of in­tel­lec­tual hon­esty. {022-S04} He redid his val­u­a­tion: as Varma re­mem­bers it, from about $5 bil­lion to about $28 bil­lion. {#valuation}

quote.text: When you’re doing some­thing so new, you can­not look at what ex­ists.

third.head: Not a Kodak moment

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Netflix and Kodak

body: Netflix began in 1997 as a DVD rental busi­ness[[x2]]. In 2007 it shipped its bil­lionth DVD; the film, Amit Varma noted for the trivia-minded, was *Babel*. {#billionth}

At that point it seemed to have cor­nered the mar­ket. “But they could have made the same mis­take that Kodak made with film,” Varma said, “and refuse to ac­cept that the world was chang­ing.” {022-S05}

Instead, under Reed Hastings, it ac­cepted the change and started a stream­ing ser­vice. Varma thinks it began by mak­ing the third sea­son of *Breaking Bad* big, then went on to com­mis­sion *House of Cards*.
For Varma, Netflix shows what lifts a busi­ness leader from good to great: the abil­ity to tell a new story about the firm. {022-C09}

quote.text: A nor­mal com­puter maker chose to jump into the world’s most com­pli­cated de­sign and man­u­fac­tur­ing prob­lem, namely CPUs. And they pulled it off.

box.title: Why firms, for Ajay Shah
box.text: Production in a mar­ket econ­omy is or­gan­ised in firms[[x5]], Ajay Shah said, and India needs firms with the pro­duc­tiv­ity[[x6]] and ca­pa­bil­i­ties of those in ad­vanced economies. He sees India’s jour­ney as syn­ony­mous with build­ing great firms. {#journey}

sections.label: The first leap
sections.head: Sun, out of Motorola’s shadow
sections.caption: Sun’s leap into CPUs
body: In the late 1980s, Ajay Shah said, Sun Microsystems made work­sta­tions from off-the-shelf parts, with CPUs bought from Motorola. Its real in­no­va­tion was the op­er­at­ing sys­tem, a vari­ant of BSD Unix from UC Berkeley brought in by its co-founder Bill Joy.

Then Motorola got stuck and could not make its CPUs faster, and Sun’s com­put­ers stalled with them. Meanwhile labs at Stanford and Berkeley were brew­ing a con­tro­ver­sial idea, re­duced in­struc­tion set com­put­ing: make the CPU very sim­ple, and it goes fast.

Sun put two and two to­gether and leapt into mak­ing CPUs. {022-S01} It in­vented an ar­chi­tec­ture called SPARC[[x7]], and for a run of about ten years it was suc­cess­ful and in­flu­en­tial. {#sparc}
## Nerve and money

Amit Varma noted that, as Clayton Christensen points out in *The Innovator’s Dilemma*, big com­pa­nies tend to get os­si­fied, with dis­rup­tion com­ing from small up­starts. {022-R07} So what, he asked, im­pressed Shah most?
“CPUs are truly hard,” Shah said. Sun also needed money, which meant in­ter­nal cash flows and the love of fi­nan­cial mar­kets. As he put it, “Wall Street tells Main Street what to do.” {022-J12}

It also had two revered en­gi­neers, Bill Joy and Andreas Bechtolsheim, who gave the firm the con­fi­dence that it could do any­thing. Varma had his own rea­son to ad­mire Joy: “Who can­not like a guy with a name like that.”
~ Sun made a sim­i­lar leap with Java, Shah noted, though no­body makes money from a pro­gram­ming lan­guage.

quote.text: A nor­mal com­puter maker chose to jump into the world’s most com­pli­cated de­sign and man­u­fac­tur­ing prob­lem, namely CPUs. And they pulled it off.

portraits.caption: Bill Joy
portraits.credit: The original uploader was SqueakBox at English Wikipedia., CC BY 2.0

sections.label: The second leap
sections.head: Beyond the search box
sections.caption: Google’s engineering culture
body: Google began as a search en­gine built on PageRank[[x8]], where, Ajay Shah noted, the “Page” is Larry Page, not a web page. Downloading and in­dex­ing the en­tire in­ter­net led it to see it­self as an in­fra­struc­ture com­pany, one that knew how to han­dle more CPUs than any­one.

The nor­mal next step was economies of scope: search for movies or music, or a search box for a company’s pri­vate data. Instead Google set out to or­gan­ise the whole world’s in­for­ma­tion, and leapt into writ­ing an op­er­at­ing sys­tem, Android. {#tagline}

Amit Varma pointed out that Larry Page and Sergey Brin started Google straight out of col­lege, be­fore cor­po­rate think­ing could in­doc­tri­nate them. It funded employees’ side projects, which he called “mas­sively plus EV” as a bet on cul­ture. {022-C03}
## Above the API

Shah’s an­swer was aes­thet­ics. Engineers see the dif­fer­ence be­tween a clean de­sign and a bad one, even when two prod­ucts look the same from out­side. A “shut up and get it done” cul­ture cre­ates bad prod­ucts in the medium term and drives away the best peo­ple. {022-C04}
Routine work can be run with in­struc­tions and tyran­ni­cal bosses, he said. Creative work above the API, where peo­ple dream and strate­gise, can­not.
~ He re­called a line from Nachiket Mor: “People re­spond to in­cen­tives, great peo­ple vol­un­teer.” {022-C06}

quote.text: So of course we need ex­e­cu­tion, but ex­e­cu­tion is com­modi­tized. And you can get ex­e­cu­tion guys a dime a dozen.

portraits.caption: Larry Page
portraits.credit: Marcin Mycielski, European Parliament (Stansfield), CC BY-SA 4.0

sections.label: The third leap
sections.head: Paise, PhDs and servers
sections.caption: Amazon’s leap into the cloud
body: Ajay Shah began his third story by de­flat­ing his sub­ject. Amazon, he said, was a book­shop, a Flipkart, a Myntra, doing “the dullest thing in the world”: putting lots of SKUs on a screen and grind­ing out de­liv­er­ies.
It was also, he said, “the big­gest re­cruiter in the whole world of PhDs in eco­nom­ics”, hired to “con you out of 35 more paise for the shirt”. {022-J04}

Then it began rent­ing out the com­put­ers it had bought for the Christmas rush, wrapped in an API. That meant build­ing some­thing as com­plex as an op­er­at­ing sys­tem, and Amazon ef­fec­tively in­vented cloud com­put­ing. {022-S03}
## Just a book­shop?

Amit Varma ob­jected. Imagining a book­shop on the in­ter­net, rather than an ac­tual book­shop, was it­self a spec­tac­u­lar leap, he said, and Jeff Bezos one of the great men of the last cou­ple of decades. Shah re­stated the ar­gu­ment, that Flipkart and Myntra were me-toos while Amazon imag­ined e-commerce it­self, and called it a fair point.

Shah also tested his own the­sis. Perhaps many firms tried au­da­cious leaps and a few suc­ceeded by dumb luck. That, he said, is why the show will never do an episode on three great fund man­agers. {022-J05}
~ Having watched these three firms for many years, he still be­lieves they were spe­cial, and he in­vited lis­ten­ers to argue the point in the com­ments. {022-C07}

quote.text: You throw 10,000 darts, 10 are going to look great.

portraits.caption: Jeff Bezos
portraits.credit: Seattle City Council from Seattle, CC BY 2.0

sections.label: The storyteller
sections.head: Once upon a valuation
sections.caption: telling a firm’s story
body: Leaps like these, Amit Varma ar­gued, are more an act of cre­ative sto­ry­telling than of lin­ear busi­ness logic. When Google said it would or­gan­ise the world’s in­for­ma­tion, that au­dac­ity mat­tered.
He drew on Aswath Damodaran’s *Narrative and Numbers*, which, he said, goes be­yond val­u­a­tion into what firms are about and the sto­ries they tell them­selves. {022-R03}

Damodaran had val­ued Uber as a taxi busi­ness. When Bill Gurley ar­gued that Uber was out to re­place car own­er­ship, Damodaran agreed and redid his sums. Something truly new, Varma said, can­not be sized by what ex­ists.
He showed a tweet by Aaron Levie: siz­ing a dis­rup­tor by the incumbent’s mar­ket “is like siz­ing the car in­dus­try of how many horses there were in 1910”. {022-C08}
## Coffee or real es­tate?

Ten years ago, Varma said, a food de­liv­ery mar­ket sized by calls to restau­rants would have looked mi­nus­cule. Then de­liv­ery changed how nu­clear fam­i­lies with two work­ing part­ners live, and cloud kitchens came up serv­ing home-like food.

Is Starbucks a cof­fee ven­dor, he asked, or in real es­tate, be­cause peo­ple need a place to sit and work? Is Walmart a re­tailer, or leas­ing space to brands? Are tech gi­ants mo­nop­o­lies, or ri­vals fight­ing for our at­ten­tion?
~ Execution and in­cen­tives make a good leader, he said; a great one also has to be a sto­ry­teller. {022-C09}

quote.text: But to be great, I think you also have to be a lit­tle bit of a sto­ry­teller.

sections.label: The reccos
sections.head: First drafts, last loves
sections.caption: making peace with first drafts
body: Amit Varma rec­om­mended Rick Rubin’s *The Creative Act* to all busi­ness­men: to suc­ceed at any­thing, he said, you need imag­i­na­tion and must think like a cre­ator. {022-R02}

He read Rubin’s line that turn­ing an idea into re­al­ity can make it seem smaller. A first draft dis­ap­points, Varma said, and a busi­ness plan meets trou­ble and piv­ots until the orig­i­nal idea is gone.

Ajay Shah said he sees it ex­actly the op­po­site way. His book with Vijay Kelkar, *In Service of the Republic*, began as a du­ti­ful primer and be­came, through page-by-page ses­sions in Pune, a cre­ative project. {#pune}
“So it ac­tu­ally goes off as an ex­po­nen­tial,” Shah said: a prod­uct starts work­man­like and be­comes more beau­ti­ful as you go. {022-C10}
## Many roads to a page

Robert Lucas, Shah said, did ten com­plete rewrites; Paul Graham, Varma added, work­shops each essay for a cou­ple of months, while George Orwell banged out three or four bril­liant col­umns a week. Varma bridged the two views with the show’s mantra, *kaator re bhaaji*: keep putting in the work, and magic can hap­pen.
~ For the stuck, he of­fered Hemingway’s cure: write one true sen­tence, then one more, true mean­ing au­then­tic to that mo­ment. {022-C12}

quote.text: But the im­por­tant thing is you have to put your bum on that chair and get the writ­ing done.
The best en­gi­neers are there to build some­thing beau­ti­ful. They’re not there to meet that KRA. They’re not there to dance to the tune of cor­po­rate HR.

p3.title: Tales of the leap
p3.deck: A phone deal, a Christmas rush, a book and a hero’s ten rewrites

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on how Android found its way to Google
stories.head: Android phones home
body: Andy Rubin had been build­ing Android, Ajay Shah said, nur­tur­ing it and build­ing it, and it was not work­ing too well. Phones of that age lacked the CPU power and bat­tery life to do any mean­ing­ful cal­cu­la­tions.
At some point Rubin ran out of steam. He was about to sell the project to a Canadian tele­com com­pany. {#canadian}

Then, in the ver­sion of the story Shah read in the press, Rubin reached out to Google late one evening. Tomorrow morn­ing, he said, he was going to sign the term sheet. But he would love it if the project went to Google, and he would go with it.
“This project re­ally be­longs in Google, that Google has the cul­ture, has the en­gi­neer­ing ca­pa­bil­ity, has the hunger to do jus­tice to Android,” Shah re­counted Rubin say­ing. {022-S02}
It was thrashed out over that evening. Google bought Rubin’s com­pany, and turned a flaky early Android into one of the most im­por­tant op­er­at­ing sys­tems in the world.

Why Google? Shah traced an old Unix cul­ture in Silicon Valley that co­a­lesced at Sun and moved through Netscape to Google. Eric Schmidt had been chief sci­en­tist at Sun; Unix leg­ends from Bell Labs, like Rob Pike, worked at Google.

~ For an en­gi­neer with the love of his life to place, Shah said, Google was the ob­vi­ous home. And for Google it was a leap like Sun’s into CPUs: a search com­pany writ­ing the most com­plex soft­ware there is.
stories.why: A strong en­gi­neer­ing cul­ture works like a mag­net: great en­gi­neers bring their best work to the firm they trust to do it jus­tice. Execution can be bought, Shah said; great leaps of ideas are scarce. {022-C05}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Android’s late-evening call

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on Amazon’s idle computers
stories.head: Christmas comes but once a year
body: Before Christmas, Ajay Shah said, Amazon saw ridicu­lous surges of de­mand. Never want­ing to turn away a cus­tomer, it sized its com­put­ers for the peak.

So for most of the year the equip­ment sat idle. Amazon was pay­ing the cost of cap­i­tal 365 days a year on ma­chines re­ally used for 10 or 15. {#capital} Then came the aha mo­ment: pack­age up that spare ca­pac­ity, wrap it in an API and rent it out to other peo­ple. {#api}

That meant build­ing some­thing as com­plex as an op­er­at­ing sys­tem, which a Flipkart or a Myntra would flat out refuse, Shah said. Amazon did it, and ef­fec­tively in­vented cloud com­put­ing, which it still dom­i­nates. {022-S03}
~ Shah still looks back in won­der, he said, that a book­shop turned into one of the im­por­tant com­puter sci­ence cor­po­ra­tions of the world.
stories.why: A cost headache, idle servers, be­came a world-changing busi­ness be­cause Amazon did not let its self-image as an e-commerce shop limit what it at­tempted. A typ­i­cal firm, in Shah’s telling, would have said “that’s not our ca­pa­bil­ity”.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the Christmas servers

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on writing a book with Vijay Kelkar
stories.head: The chore that came alive
body: When Ajay Shah and Vijay Kelkar started *In Service of the Republic*[[x9]], the aim was mod­est: a primer car­ry­ing knowl­edge from pub­lic ad­min­is­tra­tion to econ­o­mists, and from eco­nom­ics to pub­lic ad­min­is­tra­tors. It was a chore, Shah said, done as a re­spon­si­bil­ity.
Around 20 chap­ters deep, he was not hav­ing fun. {#chapters}

Their method was to re­vise and re­vise. Then Shah would carry a phys­i­cal hard copy to Pune, and the two would spend a half day or a full day walk­ing through every page. {#pune} Twenty ideas would come up, and each in­no­va­tion fed on the next until the chore be­came a cre­ative project.
~ The lan­guage im­proves the same way, Shah said: on the first draft it is al­ways bad, and around the 15th re­write it be­comes good. {#rewrite}

quote.text: So I al­ways love my ba­bies much bet­ter at the end than at the be­gin­ning.

stories.postscript: “Because young ba­bies are a pain,” Amit Varma replied. {022-J07}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on writing with Vijay Kelkar

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on how a master economist wrote
stories.head: Bin it and begin again
body: Robert Lucas, the econ­o­mist who had died re­cently, is one of Ajay Shah’s he­roes. Shah puts him in Milton Friedman’s league for the beauty of his writ­ing, and spent a lot of time study­ing how both men wrote.
Then one day Lucas said that any ar­ti­cle re­quired ten com­plete rewrites[[x10]]: lit­er­ally throw­ing a draft away and writ­ing it all over again from scratch. {#lucas}
“And that was an eye opener for me,” Shah said, “and it helped me to make peace with the crappy stuff that I do at the early stages.” {022-S07}
~ All prod­ucts start out bad, he said, and you have to shoe-leather them, mak­ing them bet­ter and bet­ter. When the sparks of life come in, the hard-working phase ends and the joy starts.
stories.why: A master’s early drafts are bad too, which frees the rest of us from de­spair. Amit Varma added that meth­ods dif­fer, from Paul Graham’s months of work­shop­ping to George Orwell’s weekly col­umns, but the bum must meet the chair. {022-C11}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Robert Lucas’s ten rewrites

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 22. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Robert Lucas (Centro de Estudios Públicos, CC BY 3.0); Bill Joy (The original uploader was SqueakBox at English Wikipedia., CC BY 2.0); Larry Page (Marcin Mycielski, European Parliament (Stansfield), CC BY-SA 4.0); Sergey Brin (Steve Jurvetson, CC BY 2.0); Jeff Bezos (Seattle City Council from Seattle, CC BY 2.0); Rick Rubin (Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 3.0); George Orwell (Cassowary Colorizations, CC BY 2.0); Ernest Hemingway (Lloyd Arnold, public domain); Clayton Christensen (World Economic Forum from Cologny, Switzerland, CC BY-SA 2.0). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon.

shelf.title: The Soul of a New Machine
shelf.creator: Tracy Kidder
shelf.why: A jour­nal­ist em­bed­ded with a Data General team build­ing a CPU takes you into the minds of the en­gi­neers and their leader, Tom West, in­clud­ing the empti­ness once the quest was over.

shelf.title: The Creative Act
shelf.creator: Rick Rubin
shelf.why: Amit rec­om­mends it to all busi­ness­men.

shelf.title: Narrative and Numbers
shelf.creator: Aswath Damodaran
shelf.why: Amit says it makes a pro­found point that goes be­yond val­u­a­tion, into what firms are about and the sto­ries they tell them­selves.

shelf.title: Uber Isn’t Worth $17 Billion
shelf.creator: Aswath Damodaran
shelf.why: The first half of the episode’s val­u­a­tion para­ble: a care­ful anal­y­sis built on what turned out to be the wrong story.

shelf.title: How to Miss By a Mile: An Alternative Look at Uber’s Potential Market Size
shelf.creator: Bill Gurley
shelf.why: Gurley ar­gued that Uber was out to re­place car own­er­ship, not just com­pete with taxis.

shelf.title: Possible, Plausible and Probable: Big markets and Networking effects
shelf.creator: Aswath Damodaran
shelf.why: Damodaran openly con­ceded that Gurley was right and redid his val­u­a­tion based on the new story.

shelf.title: The Innovator’s Dilemma
shelf.creator: Clayton Christensen
shelf.why: Why dom­i­nant com­pa­nies like Kodak can have the know-how to adapt yet fail, trapped by their own pro­cesses, pri­or­i­ties and in­cen­tives, while dis­rup­tion comes from small up­starts.

shelf.title: Essays
shelf.creator: George Orwell
shelf.why: Orwell’s non­fic­tion, which Amit prefers to the nov­els: a chrono­log­i­cal look at Orwell the thinker, who banged out three or four bril­liant col­umns a week.

shelf.title: Paul Graham’s essays
shelf.creator: Paul Graham
shelf.why: Free es­says that Amit calls ‘a trea­sure given to mankind’: mod­els of sim­ple, clear writ­ing, each work­shopped for months, by some­one who also builds things.

shelf.title: Ernest Hemingway, The Art of Fiction No. 21 (Paris Review interview)
shelf.creator: George Plimpton
shelf.why: Hemingway’s rem­edy for being stuck: sit down, write one true sen­tence, then one more.

shelf.title: A Movable Feast
shelf.creator: Ernest Hemingway
shelf.why: Source of Hemingway’s one-true-sentence ad­vice, which Amit reads as writ­ing some­thing au­then­tic to the mo­ment.

shelf.title: The Greatest Productivity Mantra: Kaator Re Bhaaji!
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The show’s pro­duc­tiv­ity mantra: be­tween a great idea and its re­al­i­sa­tion lies drudgery, and the rem­edy is to keep doing the work until magic hap­pens.

shelf.title: In Service of the Republic
shelf.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ frame­work for Indian eco­nomic pol­icy: when the state should step in, why its fail­ures cut across every do­main (HR, con­tract­ing, bud­get­ing, checks on co­er­cive power), and why the fix is checks and bal­ances and small, re­versible steps.

shelf.title: On Diversification by Firms
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Background on the con­ven­tional paths of firm ex­pan­sion that the three great leaps break from.

shelf.title: Economies of Scale, Economies of Scope
shelf.creator: Venkatesh Rao
shelf.why: Explains the two text­book growth paths (doing more of the same, or mov­ing into ad­ja­cen­cies) against which Sun, Google and Amazon look so au­da­cious.

shelf.title: The Network is the Computer
shelf.creator: Bradford Morgan White
shelf.why: Further read­ing on the com­pany whose leap into CPUs opens the episode.

shelf.title: The Friendship That Made Google Huge
shelf.creator: James Somers
shelf.why: Further read­ing on the en­gi­neer­ing cul­ture that, in Ajay’s telling, let Google han­dle the world’s largest com­put­ing prob­lems.

shelf.title: I, Robot: The Man Behind the Google Phone
shelf.creator: John Markoff
shelf.why: Further read­ing on Andy Rubin, the cen­tral fig­ure in the Android leap.

shelf.title: How Amazon grew an awkward side project into AWS, a behemoth that’s now 4 times bigger than its original shopping business
shelf.creator: Geoff Colvin
shelf.why: Further read­ing on how a bookshop’s in­ter­nal in­fra­struc­ture turned into the cloud com­put­ing busi­ness.

shelf.title: Don’t Get Fooled by Success
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s col­umn on sur­vivor­ship bias: a fund’s track record can be pure luck, so don’t read suc­cess sto­ries as proof of ge­nius when many sim­i­lar at­tempts may have failed un­seen.

shelf.title: Two great investment strategies
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s older piece on in­vest­ing, a cau­tion that sto­ries of great fund man­agers are mostly sur­vivor­ship bias and that track records can mis­lead.

laughs.text: The open­ing ‘mys­tery hunt’: Ajay had once claimed to be an ex­pert in six­teen things, and Amit re­ports that ‘the in­ter­net is abuzz, mat­ters have gone viral, hash­tags have been formed. Tell me at least one more of those six­teen things.’ Ajay’s an­swer: firms.
Amit’s pun: ‘I see that you have made a firm re­solve to talk about firms today.’
Amit after the Sun story: ‘Also, what a great name, Bill Joy, who can­not like a guy with a name like that.’

Ajay’s por­trait of re­tail Amazon as ‘the big­gest re­cruiter in the whole world of PhDs in eco­nom­ics who will find every be­hav­ioral eco­nom­ics bug in your be­hav­ior and con you out of 35 more paise for the shirt.’
Ajay on sur­vivor­ship bias: ‘we’re never going to do a show here say­ing three great fund man­agers.’
Ajay: ‘I al­ways love my ba­bies much bet­ter at the end than at the be­gin­ning.’ Amit: ‘Because young ba­bies are a pain.’
Amit’s sign-off asks view­ers what they think of the firms dis­cussed, and then ‘the most im­por­tant thing, what do you think of Ajay’s shirt?’
PageRank, Google’s found­ing al­go­rithm, where the ‘Page’ refers not to a web page but to Larry Page.

RISC vs com­plex in­struc­tion set com­put­ing: the late-1980s idea from Stanford and Berkeley labs that rad­i­cally sim­pler CPUs would run faster, which Sun bet on with its SPARC ar­chi­tec­ture against Intel and Motorola.

The Silicon Valley Unix lin­eage Ajay traces from Sun to Netscape to Google: Eric Schmidt went from chief sci­en­tist at Sun to Netscape, and Rob Pike from the orig­i­nal Bell Labs Unix team works at Google.
Ajay’s aside while ex­plain­ing how Sun funded its CPU leap: ‘Wall Street tells Main Street what to do.’

Netflix trivia from Amit: the bil­lionth DVD it shipped, in 2007, was Babel. He con­trasts Netflix’s move into stream­ing (Breaking Bad, then House of Cards) with Kodak’s fail­ure to ac­cept that film was dying.
Ajay para­phrased Hemingway as get­ting one sen­tence right to light up your day. Amit cor­rected it to ‘one true sen­tence,’ from Hemingway’s Paris Review in­ter­view about writer’s block.
